Zeppelin
ZEP-uh-lin
noun (eponym: Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin)
From a proper name, per the Oxford English Dictionary: Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin (1838–1917), the German general and inventor of the rigid airship. The OED records its earliest evidence in 1896, in the Washington Post.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A zeppelin is a rigid airship: a long frame covered in fabric and lifted by gas-filled cells inside it. The word is named for Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin, a German general whose name became synonymous with airships, which dominated long-distance flight until the 1930s. His interest began, by his own later account, in America. In 1863 he took leave to observe the Union’s Army of the Potomac in Virginia, and afterward, travelling in Minnesota, he made his first ascent in a balloon with the itinerant balloonist John Steiner at St. Paul. On 2 July 1900 he made the first flight of his LZ 1 over Lake Constance; it stayed up for twenty minutes and was damaged on landing. The Christian observation: men had long watched the clouds before they rode them, and Scripture gives the clouds to God as His chariot: He “maketh the clouds his chariot: who walketh upon the wings of the wind” (Psa 104:3). Every human flight is borrowed lift. The higher promise is to those who wait on the LORD: “they shall mount up with wings as eagles” (Isa 40:31). And a man may plan his voyage, but “the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

A rigid airship, named for Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin, who first rose in a balloon at St. Paul after observing the Civil War in Virginia (OED earliest 1896; first flight 1900). He maketh the clouds his chariot (Psa 104:3).

ZEPPELIN, n. (from 1896, OED) A large rigid airship with a covered framework containing gas cells. From Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin (1838–1917).

History note: observer with the Army of the Potomac in Virginia, 1863; first flight of LZ 1, 2 July 1900 (Wikipedia, “Ferdinand von Zeppelin”).

Key Scripture

Psa 104:3 — "Who layeth the beams of his chambers in the waters: who maketh the clouds his chariot: who walketh upon the wings of the wind:"

Isa 40:31 — "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint."

Pro 16:9 — "A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps."

Modern Corruption

Man learned to ride the clouds God made His chariot; the temptation of every age of flight is to think the sky now belongs to us.

expand to see more

The airship was a triumph, and for a generation it ruled long-distance flight. Then its age ended. Human mastery of the air has moved on many times since, and each step brings the same temptation: to look down from a height and imagine we have climbed beyond the need of God.

Scripture keeps the clouds in God’s hand (Psa 104:3) and puts the true rising elsewhere, in the strength given to those who wait on the LORD (Isa 40:31). A man devises his way; the LORD directs his steps (Pro 16:9).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin (1838–1917) → balloon ascent at St. Paul, 1863 → LZ 1, 1900 → zeppelin (OED earliest 1896) → any rigid airship.
